messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi Patel was 53 when his partner’s younger brother died suddenly in a house fire after what the family later understood had been a night of heavy drinking. Ravi had been the person everyone relied on in a crisis: the steady one, the analyst who noticed details, made quick decisions, and kept his head. That night he arrived to smoke, shouting, and the harsh chemical-burnt smell of a kitchen already engulfed. Someone nearby had spilled liquor; even now, what stays with him is the sickening mix of alcohol on the air and scorched heat. He remembers fragments with unnatural vividness—the orange flicker reflected in a window, his own hand slipping on a railing, a shout that may have been his partner’s—but the sequence will not hold together. There are blank stretches he cannot recover at all. What he can recall does not feel concluded. When it comes back, it is not like remembering; it is as if he is standing there again, urgently trying to work out what to do before it is too late.

In the months afterward, Ravi became increasingly preoccupied with what the night meant about him. He had always seen himself as competent and dependable, someone whose judgment under pressure defined him. Now he had come to believe that this image had been exposed as false. He was certain that if he had truly been capable, he would have known what to do, moved faster, chosen differently. The very gaps in his memory seemed, to him, like proof of weakness rather than shock. Not being able to reconstruct the event left him doubting his own mind, and the way the memory arrived in jagged pieces only deepened his conviction that he could not trust himself to do the right thing when it mattered. He began to say, quietly and with shame, that he was no longer the man he had been.

Those beliefs altered what he noticed around him. At work as a cybersecurity analyst, he had once been comfortable talking about long-term projects, promotions, and plans for the next quarter. Now even casual conversations about the future—where he and his partner might travel, whether they should think about retirement, what a team rollout might look like six months ahead—caught him sharply. The future no longer felt like something he could enter with confidence. It felt like a demand to imagine himself as reliable and effective, and he did not believe that version of himself existed anymore. In the office break room, if a colleague reheated something until it singed, the burnt smell would stop him mid-thought. If he passed a cluster of coworkers joking over drinks after hours, the smell of alcohol could make his body tense before he had consciously registered why.

When those moments came, the memory did not stay in the past. The smell of burnt food or liquor seemed to pull the event forward intact, and he would suddenly be back in the night of the fire, with no protective sense of distance. At his desk, staring at network logs, he could lose several minutes to an image of flame under a doorframe or to a disconnected impression of shouting in a stairwell. Just as often, the memory itself primed him to scan for those cues. After a morning of intrusive recollections, he would find himself noticing every faint smoky odor in the building, every mention of weekend drinking, every conversation that leaned toward what was coming next in life. His world had narrowed around these signals, as though the memory kept teaching him where danger lived, and those signals in turn reopened the memory with full force.

The more often this happened, the more convinced Ravi became that something fundamental in him had failed. Being thrown without warning into a scene that felt current and immediate left him shaken and ashamed; afterward he would think, a strong person would not come apart like this. When he could not fill in the missing parts, he took that as further evidence that he was incapable. And because he believed he could not trust himself, anticipation itself became fraught: a future plan, a family conversation about next year, even his partner asking what they should do over the holidays could set his nerves on edge before any memory had fully formed.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had begun to affect both home and work. He was still performing his job, but more rigidly, avoiding optional meetings where planning was discussed and stepping out of shared spaces if he caught the smell of alcohol or something burnt. His partner had noticed that any attempt to talk about the future made him go quiet or abruptly change the subject. Ravi came to treatment exhausted by the sense that the worst night of his life was still happening in pieces around him. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself, but the conclusion he had drawn from it: that when everything mattered, he had been weak, and that the man who once knew how to act had not come back. He said he wanted help finding out whether the night had truly revealed who he was, or whether he had been living inside that moment for so long that he could no longer tell the difference.
